Cost-sensitive learning: higher cost for minority misclassification. Combine techniques. Stratified split: preserve class distribution in train/test.

question: Explain hyperparameter tuning and cross-validation together.
ideal_answer: Hyperparameters (not learned from data): learning rate, regularization, tree depth. Tuning finds optimal values. GridSearchCV tries all combinations; RandomizedSearchCV samples randomly. Cross-validation evaluates each combination using multiple train-test splits (avoids overfitting to single split). Nested CV: outer loop evaluates; inner loop tunes. Time-consuming. Start with defaults, coarse search, fine search. Early stopping monitors validation loss, stops training if no improvement. Nested CV more robust but expensive; outer CV estimates generalization.

question: Explain the curse of dimensionality.
ideal_answer: Curse of dimensionality: as features increase, data becomes sparse and high-dimensional. Problems: 1) more data needed for same coverage (exponential growth), 2) distances become meaningless (all equidistant), 3) overfitting (more features = more parameters), 4) computation expensive, 5) visualization impossible. Example: 100 features, training 10^100 points to cover space. Solutions: feature selection (remove irrelevant), dimensionality reduction (PCA), regularization, domain knowledge. Trade-off: fewer features = better generalization, but may lose information. Relevant for distance-based (KNN, SVM, clustering) and high-dimensional data.

question: Explain A/B testing and statistical significance.
ideal_answer: A/B testing compares two versions (A: control, B: treatment). Randomly assign users to versions. Measure metric (conversion, retention, etc.). Test for statistical significance using hypothesis test. Null: no difference. If p < 0.05, reject null (significant difference). Multiple comparisons problem: more tests = higher false positive rate (correct with Bonferroni). Sample size calculation: power (probability of detecting true effect), significance level (alpha), effect size. Common pitfall: stopping early when significant (p-hacking). Valid when: random assignment, sufficient sample size, pre-registered hypothesis.

question: Explain effect size and its importance.
ideal_answer: Effect size measures magnitude of difference (e.g., between groups). P-value shows significance (existence of effect); effect size shows importance. Common measures: Cohen's d (difference in means / std dev), correlation coefficient, odds ratio. Small d=0.2, medium d=0.5, large d=0.8. Important for: interpreting results (statistical vs practical significance), planning studies (power analysis), meta-analysis. P-value depends on sample size (large samples show significance for tiny effects). Effect size independent of sample size. Report both p-value and effect size.

question: Explain time series analysis and seasonality/trend.
ideal_answer: Time series: data ordered by time. Trend: long-term direction (increasing/decreasing). Seasonality: repeating patterns (daily, monthly, yearly). Noise: random variation. Decomposition separates components. ARIMA (AutoRegressive Integrated Moving Average) models trends. Seasonal decomposition identifies patterns. Lagging: using previous values as features. Autocorrelation: correlation with past values. Challenges: non-stationarity (mean/variance change), missing values, handling future. Forecasting: predict future values. Applications: stock prices, weather, demand, sensor data. Time series CV maintains temporal order (no future leakage).

question: Explain data visualization importance and choose appropriate plots.
ideal_answer: Visualization reveals patterns, outliers, trends faster than numbers. Plot types: histogram (distribution), scatter (relationships), box plot (outliers, quartiles), heatmap (2D data, correlations), line plot (trends), bar chart (categories). Tools: Matplotlib, Seaborn, Plotly. Principles: appropriate chart for data, clear labels, avoid distortion, color blindness-friendly. Exploratory: understand data. Explanatory: communicate insights. Storytelling: guide viewer through insights. Design: minimize cognitive load. Accessibility: legends, annotations. Interactive plots (Plotly, D3) explore data dynamically.

question: Explain model interpretability and explainability.
ideal_answer: Interpretability: understanding why model makes prediction. Explainability: explaining decision to others. Importance: regulatory (GDPR), user trust, debugging. Techniques: feature importance (tree models), SHAP values (game theory, model-agnostic), LIME (local approximation), attention weights (neural networks), coefficients (linear models). Black-box vs interpretable: neural networks harder to interpret; decision trees transparent. Trade-off: interpretability vs accuracy (often inverse). New regulations require explanation. Explainability techniques increasingly developed.

question: Explain model validation, evaluation metrics, and overfitting.
ideal_answer: Validation estimates generalization to new data. Train/test split (single evaluation). Cross-validation (multiple splits, average). Holdout validation set (for hyperparameter tuning). Metrics: regression (MAE, RMSE, R²), classification (accuracy, precision, recall, F1, ROC-AUC). Overfitting: model memorizes training data. Signs: high train accuracy, low test accuracy. Underfitting: model too simple. Solutions: regularization, cross-validation, more data, simpler model. Learning curves: plot train/test accuracy vs data size (diagnose bias/variance). Confusion matrix: true/false positives/negatives.

question: Explain time-based operations in Pandas: resample, rolling, expanding.
ideal_answer: Resample changes frequency: df.resample('D').sum() daily totals. Upsampling (frequent) vs downsampling (less frequent). Rolling computes moving statistics: df['price'].rolling(window=7).mean() 7-day moving average. Min_periods parameter includes partial windows. Expanding: df['price'].expanding().mean() cumulative average. Shift: df['price'].shift(1) previous value (NaN for first). Diff: df['price'].diff() change from previous. Pct_change: percentage change. Essential for time series analysis. DatetimeIndex needed for time operations.

question: Explain Pandas multi-indexing (hierarchical index).
ideal_answer: Multi-index (hierarchical) organizes data by multiple levels. Create: df = pd.DataFrame(..., index=pd.MultiIndex.from_tuples(...)). Access: df.loc[('level1_val', 'level2_val')]. Unstack/stack convert between multi-index and wide/long format. Level names aid clarity. Sorting: sort_index(level=0). Swaplevel: exchange index level order. Benefits: organizes complex data, enables groupby on index. Useful for time series (date, ticker), cross-sections (country, year).

question: Explain NumPy's linear algebra operations: dot, matrix multiplication, eigenvalues.
ideal_answer: np.dot(a, b) computes dot product (1D) or matrix multiplication (2D). @operator equivalent: a @ b (Python 3.5+). np.linalg.inv(matrix) computes inverse. np.linalg.det(matrix) determinant. np.linalg.eig(matrix) eigenvalues/eigenvectors. Svd: np.linalg.svd(matrix) singular value decomposition. Norm: np.linalg.norm(vector) vector magnitude. Solving linear systems: np.linalg.solve(A, b) solves Ax=b. Cholesky decomposition: np.linalg.cholesky(matrix). Important for: optimization, dimensionality reduction, machine learning. NumPy wraps LAPACK (fast, optimized).

question: Explain feature importance and model interpretability in Scikit-learn.
ideal_answer: Tree-based models (RandomForest, XGBoost) provide feature_importances_. Example: model.fit(X, y); importances = model.feature_importances_. Measures: Gini/entropy importance (split frequency), permutation importance (drop feature, measure performance loss). Permutation more reliable: from sklearn.inspection import permutation_importance. Coefficient interpretation for linear models: positive = feature increases prediction, magnitude = strength. Careful: correlation vs causation. SHAP values model-agnostic explanation. Feature importance guides feature selection, debugging, business insights.

question: Explain model selection and comparison strategies.
ideal_answer: Cross-validation compares models: cross_val_score(model1, X, y) vs cross_val_score(model2, X, y). Statistical test: paired t-test if scores from same folds. Nested CV: outer for evaluation, inner for hyperparameter tuning. Hold out test set: final evaluation on unseen data (don't use for tuning). Metrics: baseline model (simple, interpretable), complex model (ensemble). Calibration plot: predicted vs actual probability. Learning curves: diagnose bias/variance. Complexity: simpler models preferred (Occam's razor) if similar performance.

question: Explain transfer learning and fine-tuning.
ideal_answer: Transfer learning uses pre-trained models (trained on large dataset like ImageNet) on new task. Advantages: faster training, requires less data, better performance. Approaches: use pre-trained features (freeze layers, train final layers only), fine-tune (unfreeze layers, train with low learning rate). Example: load ResNet50 (trained on ImageNet), replace final layer with custom output, fine-tune on medical images. Layer freezing: freeze early layers (general features), train later layers (specific to task). Learning rate lower for fine-tuning (avoid overwriting learned features). State-of-the-art for image/NLP tasks when data limited.

question: Explain batch size and its effect on training.
ideal_answer: Batch size: number of samples per gradient update. Larger batch: smoother gradient (stable), faster computation, but may get stuck in local minima. Smaller batch: noisier gradient (may escape local minima), slower, more memory-efficient per batch but more iterations. Trade-off: stability vs exploration. Typical: 32, 64, 128, 256. GPU memory limits batch size. Batch normalization reduces sensitivity to batch size. Learning rate interacts with batch size (larger batches may need smaller learning rate). Momentum/Adam optimizers handle varying batches. Micro-batching: gradient accumulation (simulate larger batch without more memory).

question: Explain common Scikit-learn model types and when to use each.
ideal_answer: Linear models: LinearRegression (fast, interpretable), LogisticRegression (classification), Ridge/Lasso (regularization). Tree models: DecisionTreeClassifier (interpretable, fast), RandomForestClassifier (robust, high-dimensional). Distance: KNeighborsClassifier (simple, no training), SVM (powerful, needs scaling). Ensemble: VotingClassifier (combine models), GradientBoostingClassifier (strong). Unsupervised: KMeans (clustering), PCA (dimensionality reduction). Start with simple (linear), move to complex if needed. Combination: ensemble (voting, stacking). Domain knowledge guides selection.

question: Explain two-pointer technique and sliding window.
ideal_answer: Two-pointer: maintain pointers at start/end, move toward center or solve problems. Example: sorted two-sum (find pair summing to target). Left pointer at start, right at end, move based on sum vs target. Efficient for: sorted arrays, linked lists, partitioning. Sliding window: maintain window of elements, slide right boundary, shrink left boundary. Example: longest substring without repeating characters. Efficient for: subarray problems, pattern matching. Both avoid nested loops (O(n²) → O(n)). Requires understanding problem structure.

question: Explain DFS and BFS difference and use cases.
ideal_answer: DFS (Depth-First Search): explore deeply before backtracking. Stack-based (implicit in recursion). Example: visit root, go deep in first child, backtrack. Use cases: topological sort, cycle detection, path problems. BFS (Breadth-First Search): explore level-by-level. Queue-based. Example: visit all neighbors before going deeper. Use cases: shortest path (unweighted), connected components, level-by-level traversal. DFS: simpler (recursion), less memory (stack vs queue). BFS: finds shortest path (unweighted). Time both O(V+E); space differs. Choose based on problem.

question: Explain backtracking and provide examples (N-Queens, Sudoku).
ideal_answer: Backtracking: explore all possible solutions, abandon path when it can't lead to solution. Recursive with constraint checking. Example N-Queens: place queen on row, check column/diagonal constraints, recursively place next row. If no valid position, backtrack (try previous placement). Example Sudoku: fill cell, check row/column/box constraints, recursively fill next cell. Backtrack if contradiction. Efficient than brute-force (prune invalid branches). Time: potentially exponential (worst case all solutions). Used for constraint satisfaction problems, permutations, combinatorics.

question: What are your career goals?
ideal_answer: Be specific, realistic, time-bound. Example: 5-year goal: lead ML engineering team, mentor junior engineers, impact production systems at scale. Next 1-2 years: deepen deployment expertise, lead cross-functional projects. Align with role: this role a step toward goals? Show ambition but not restlessness. Avoid: different field (suggests you'll leave), too vague, unrealistic. Company wants: will you grow with us or get bored? Staying and contributing? Connect to company values/opportunities. Growth path within company attractive. Flexibility shows you think long-term.
